SECTION B: Respiratory Pathology MCQ CAT 1 (23rd March 2026)
This article provides a high-yield overview of frequently tested yet often "missed" topics in respiratory pathology, designed to complement a broader study of the respiratory system.

qs.q: Which respiratory pathology topic is covered during the second semester modules?
qs.e: Acute Lung Injury and Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome are listed under the Pathology of the Respiratory System. Peptic ulcer disease belongs to the gastrointestinal system module.

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Respiratory pathology covers diseases that damage airways, lung parenchyma, pleura or vasculature, leading to impaired gas exchange. Clinicians must link symptoms, risk factors and investigations to identify the underlying process and its severity.

sections.p: Respiratory pathology refers to any structural or functional abnormality of the respiratory system that causes clinical disease. Diagnosis combines history, physical exam, imaging and targeted tests.
b: Identify pattern: obstructive, restrictive, vascular, infectious, neoplastic.
Use WHO criteria for TB, GOLD criteria for COPD, Berlin definition for ARDS.

sections.p: Severity guides treatment and prognosis. Established staging systems include GOLD for COPD, WHO for TB, and the PaO2/FiO2 ratio for ARDS.
b: Mild COPD: FEV1 ≥80% predicted; severe: <30%.
TB: smear‑positive vs smear‑negative, drug‑resistant categories.

sections.p: Causes are grouped by anatomic location and epidemiology. In low‑resource settings, infections and environmental exposures dominate.
b: Obstructive: smoking, biomass fuel, HIV‑related bronchitis.
Restrictive: silicosis, post‑TB fibrosis, sarcoidosis.
Infectious: TB, bacterial pneumonia, malaria‑related pulmonary edema.

sections.p: Patients present with dyspnea, cough, sputum, chest pain or hemoptysis. The timing, triggers and associated systemic signs narrow the differential.
b: Acute dyspnea + fever → infection or pulmonary embolism.
Progressive cough + weight loss → TB or malignancy.

sections.p: Select tests that answer a specific clinical question; when unavailable, use bedside alternatives.

t.b: What structural abnormality is present? Shows infiltrates, hyperinflation, cavitation; if unavailable, use ultrasound for pleural effusion.
Is the defect obstructive or restrictive? Low FEV1/FVC indicates obstruction; reduced total lung capacity indicates restriction.
Is Mycobacterium tuberculosis present? Positive result confirms TB; negative does not rule out in HIV patients.
Is gas exchange impaired? Low PaO2 or high PaCO2 guides oxygen/ventilatory support.

sections.p: Recognize features that signal imminent deterioration or life‑threatening complications.
b: Sudden worsening dyspnea with chest pain → pulmonary embolism.
Severe hypoxemia (PaO2 <60 mmHg) despite oxygen.
Massive hemoptysis >200 mL/24 h.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care and monitor response.
b: COPD exacerbation: inhaled bronchodilators, systemic steroids, antibiotics if infection suspected.
TB: standard 2HRZE/4HR regimen; avoid monotherapy to prevent resistance.
Pneumonia: empiric antibiotics covering typical and atypical organisms; adjust for local resistance patterns.

sections.p: Regular review prevents progression and detects complications early.
b: COPD: annual spirometry, smoking cessation counseling.
TB: sputum check at 2 months, adherence support.
Vaccination: influenza, pneumococcal for high‑risk patients.

sections.p: Conditions that share similar symptoms or imaging findings.
b: COPD vs asthma – reversibility and age of onset differ.
TB vs lung cancer – both cause cavitary lesions; biopsy clarifies.

sections.p: Pitfalls in interpretation that may lead to misdiagnosis.
b: Normal chest X‑ray early in HIV‑related TB.
Spirometry may appear normal in early restrictive disease; consider lung volumes.

whenToSeekHelp: Chest pain radiating to arm or jaw
Unexplained collapse or loss of consciousness

faq.a: Smoking recruits neutrophils/macrophages that release elastase, which destroys alveolar walls when α1‑antitrypsin is overwhelmed.
Airway obstruction is largely irreversible; treatment reduces symptoms and slows progression.

faq.q: When is a chest X‑ray insufficient?
faq.a: Early TB in HIV or small pulmonary emboli may be missed; consider CT or ultrasound if suspicion remains high.

exam: Explain the GOLD classification for COPD and its clinical implications.
List the first‑line diagnostic steps for a patient with chronic cough in a TB‑endemic region.
Describe how you would differentiate acute bacterial pneumonia from pulmonary edema on imaging and labs.
